The strike involved a broad range of employees—including nurses, technicians, pharmacists, and support staff—at hundreds of Kaiser facilities across California, Colorado, Oregon, Washington, Virginia, and Washington, D.C. The union coalition had issued a 10-day strike notice on September 22, 2023, after their previous contracts expired on September 30 without a new agreement. [2, 3] The vote came after months of stalled negotiations, with union leaders arguing that management's proposals on wages would worsen an existing staffing crisis. This was the third time the court had set aside regulations related to the act. Siding with the Texas Medical Association (TMA), the court found that the methodology for calculating the qualifying payment amount (QPA) unfairly favored insurers. The ruling specifically disallowed several regulatory provisions, including those that permitted insurers to factor in "ghost rates" (contracted rates for services not actually provided by a specific provider) and out-of-specialty rates in the QPA calculation. It also struck down the provision allowing self-insured group health plans to use rates from all plans managed by their third-party administrator, which the TMA argued tilted the arbitration process in insurers’ favor. Following the ruling, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) announced it was once again pausing all federal independent dispute resolution (IDR) processes. <6> CVS Health announced the launch of Cordavis, a wholly owned subsidiary, on August 23, 2023. [1, 2] The new company will work directly with manufacturers to commercialize and co-produce biosimilar drugs to increase competition and lower costs in the U.S. pharmaceutical market. [1, 2, 7] Cordavis's first product, developed in partnership with Sandoz, will be a biosimilar of Humira called Hyrimoz. [1, 3] It is scheduled to launch in the first quarter of 2024 with a list price that is more than 80% lower than Humira's current price. [1, 2]

Furthermore, nearly half of adults in the U.S. delay or skip medical care due to high costs. The survey of 2,663 adults highlighted that medical debt has considerable effects on both physical and mental health, with 42% of those with debt delaying further medical care and nearly a third reporting increased depression and anxiety. The proposed changes aim to streamline operations and ensure more timely payment determinations by resolving disputes between healthcare providers and insurers. Key proposals include requiring insurers to provide more detailed information with initial payments or denials, enhancing the open negotiation process through a federal portal, and modifying the requirements for batching multiple items into a single dispute, with a proposed limit of 25 items. The survey, which included individuals with employer, marketplace, individual-market, Medicaid, and Medicare plans, revealed that inadequate coverage often leads to delaying or forgoing necessary medical care and prescriptions. These subsidies, originally expanded by the American Rescue Plan, contribute to making coverage more affordable. The strike was a response to failed contract negotiations concerning what the Coalition of Kaiser Permanente Unions described as unfair labor practices and critical understaffing levels that jeopardize patient safety. The strike involved a broad range of employees—including nurses, technicians, pharmacists, and support staff—at hundreds of Kaiser facilities across California, Colorado, Oregon, Washington, Virginia, and Washington, D.C. The union coalition had issued a 10-day strike notice on September 22, 2023, after their previous contracts expired on September 30 without a new agreement. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> Following a temporary suspension due to legal challenges, the federal independent dispute resolution (IDR) portal fully reopened for all dispute types on December 15, 2023. The closure was a result of a court ruling, TMA IV, which invalidated certain aspects of the No Surprises Act's IDR process, including the administrative fee structure. This full reopening, announced by the Departments of Health and Human Services, Labor, and Treasury, followed a partial reopening in October 2023 for new single and bundled claims. <2> By the end of June 2023, the federal independent dispute resolution (IDR) process, initiated in April 2022 under the No Surprises Act, was inundated with approximately 490,000 dispute cases. This volume far surpassed the government's initial annual estimates of 17,000 to 22,000 cases, creating a substantial backlog with about 61% of disputes, or nearly 300,000 cases, remaining unresolved. The high number of disputes, filed predominantly by a small number of healthcare provider organizations, exposed significant administrative hurdles, including a burdensome online portal, difficulties in determining case eligibility, and restrictive batching rules. These challenges contributed to a median case resolution time of 76 days, far exceeding the 30-day statutory requirement. The system's implementation also led to higher-than-expected costs; providers were reportedly winning a majority of disputes and receiving payments nearly three times the usual in-network rates, creating significant financial implications for payers. <3> On December 12, 2023, the U.S. House of Representatives passed the Support for Patients and Communities Reauthorization Act (H.R. 4531) with a strong bipartisan vote of 386 to 37. This legislation reauthorizes and modifies a range of programs aimed at preventing and treating substance use disorders (SUD). Key provisions include renewing support for individuals in SUD treatment and recovery, enhancing resources for residential treatment for pregnant and postpartum women, and permanently extending required Medicaid coverage for medication-assisted treatments. On the same day, the Senate Health, Education, Labor & Pensions (HELP) Committee also advanced its version of the bill, S. 3393, with a 19-1 vote, signaling bipartisan consensus in both chambers on the need to address the ongoing opioid crisis. <4> On December 11, 2023, the U.S. House of Representatives passed the 'Lower Costs, More Transparency Act' (H.R. 5378) with a strong bipartisan vote of 320-71, with one member voting present. This legislation aims to increase price transparency within the healthcare system by requiring hospitals, insurers, clinical laboratories, imaging providers, and ambulatory surgical centers to publicly disclose their prices. The bill also targets Pharmacy Benefit Managers (PBMs), mandating they provide detailed reports on drug spending, rebates, and fees to health plan sponsors. Furthermore, the act includes provisions for Medicare site-neutral payment policies for certain drugs administered in off-campus hospital outpatient departments, ensuring payment is the same as in other provider settings. It also extends funding for several key public health programs, including the Teaching Health Center Graduate Medical Education Program and the National Health Service Corps. <5> The U.S. House of Representatives passed the "Lower Costs, More Transparency Act" (H.R. 5378) on December 11, 2023, with a significant bipartisan majority of 320 to 71, with one member voting present. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> A report from Patient Rights Advocate (PRA), released in February 2024, revealed a decline in hospital compliance with federal price transparency regulations. [6] The study, which analyzed 2,000 U.S. hospitals, found that only 34.5% were fully compliant with the rules as of January 2024. [6] This represents a slight decrease from the 36% compliance rate reported in July 2023. [6] The report highlighted that none of the hospitals within major systems such as HCA Healthcare and Tenet Healthcare were in full compliance. Kaiser Permanente, which had a 98% compliance rate in the previous report, dropped to 0% because its hospitals began posting multiple data files instead of a single, comprehensive one. It is worth noting that some organizations, like the American Hospital Association (AHA), have contested the methodology and accuracy of PRA's findings, pointing to CMS data that suggests a much higher compliance rate of 70%. [3] <2> A survey released by AHIP and the Blue Cross Blue Shield Association (BCBSA) on January 29, 2024, found that the No Surprises Act (NSA) protected Americans from more than 10 million surprise medical bills during the first nine months of 2023. While the act was effective in protecting patients, the report also highlighted a significant and troubling increase in the use of the Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) process. The number of initiated disputes was found to be nearly 14 times higher than initial government estimates. Between April 15, 2022, and March 31, 2023, 334,828 disputes were initiated through the IDR portal, far exceeding the 17,000 claims federal agencies had originally projected for a one-year period. A separate analysis from Families USA corroborates this, stating some health care providers and medical billing companies have inundated the IDR process. <3> A retrospective analysis of media coverage revealed a significant increase in public disputes between healthcare providers and insurers in 2023. According to research by FTI Consulting, at least 86 such disputes were reported in the media, marking a 69% surge from the 51 conflicts recorded in 2022. These disputes, spanning 34 states, frequently centered on disagreements over reimbursement rates. A prominent feature of these conflicts was the involvement of Medicare Advantage (MA) plans. In 2023, 59% of all publicly reported disputes (51 total) involved MA plans, with 12 of those disputes exclusively focused on them. This continues a trend from 2022, where 56% of disputes involved MA plans. Of the public disputes in 2023, 44% did not result in a timely agreement, leading to patients going out-of-network. <4> On December 21, 2023, the U.S. Departments of Health and Human Services (HHS), Labor, and the Treasury issued a final rule titled "Federal Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) Process Administrative Fee and Certified IDR Entity Fee Ranges." [2, 4, 5, 6] This rule, which took effect on January 22, 2024, establishes the fee structure for the independent dispute resolution process under the No Surprises Act. [4, 8, 9] The final rule sets the administrative fee at $115 per party for each dispute. [4, 10] It also establishes the permissible fee ranges for certified IDR entities, setting them at $200 to $840 for single determinations and $268 to $1,173 for batched determinations. [4, 5, 10] This action followed an August 2023 court decision that vacated a previous attempt by the departments to increase the administrative fee without undergoing the formal notice and comment rulemaking process. [5, 7, 10] <5> Following a temporary suspension due to legal challenges, the federal independent dispute resolution (IDR) portal fully reopened for all dispute types on December 15, 2023. The closure was a result of a court ruling, TMA IV, which invalidated certain aspects of the No Surprises Act's IDR process, including the administrative fee structure. This full reopening, announced by the Departments of Health and Human Services, Labor, and Treasury, followed a partial reopening in October 2023 for new single and bundled claims. <6> By the end of June 2023, the federal independent dispute resolution (IDR) process, initiated in April 2022 under the No Surprises Act, was inundated with approximately 490,000 dispute cases. This volume far surpassed the government's initial annual estimates of 17,000 to 22,000 cases, creating a substantial backlog with about 61% of disputes, or nearly 300,000 cases, remaining unresolved. The high number of disputes, filed predominantly by a small number of healthcare provider organizations, exposed significant administrative hurdles, including a burdensome online portal, difficulties in determining case eligibility, and restrictive batching rules. These challenges contributed to a median case resolution time of 76 days, far exceeding the 30-day statutory requirement. The system's implementation also led to higher-than-expected costs; providers were reportedly winning a majority of disputes and receiving payments nearly three times the usual in-network rates, creating significant financial implications for payers. <7> On December 12, 2023, the U.S. House of Representatives passed the Support for Patients and Communities Reauthorization Act (H.R. 4531) with a strong bipartisan vote of 386 to 37. This legislation reauthorizes and modifies a range of programs aimed at preventing and treating substance use disorders (SUD). Key provisions include renewing support for individuals in SUD treatment and recovery, enhancing resources for residential treatment for pregnant and postpartum women, and permanently extending required Medicaid coverage for medication-assisted treatments. On the same day, the Senate Health, Education, Labor & Pensions (HELP) Committee also advanced its version of the bill, S. 3393, with a 19-1 vote, signaling bipartisan consensus in both chambers on the need to address the ongoing opioid crisis. <8> On December 11, 2023, the U.S. House of Representatives passed the 'Lower Costs, More Transparency Act' (H.R. 5378) with a strong bipartisan vote of 320-71, with one member voting present. This legislation aims to increase price transparency within the healthcare system by requiring hospitals, insurers, clinical laboratories, imaging providers, and ambulatory surgical centers to publicly disclose their prices. The bill also targets Pharmacy Benefit Managers (PBMs), mandating they provide detailed reports on drug spending, rebates, and fees to health plan sponsors. Furthermore, the act includes provisions for Medicare site-neutral payment policies for certain drugs administered in off-campus hospital outpatient departments, ensuring payment is the same as in other provider settings. It also extends funding for several key public health programs, including the Teaching Health Center Graduate Medical Education Program and the National Health Service Corps. <9> The U.S. House of Representatives passed the "Lower Costs, More Transparency Act" (H.R. 5378) on December 11, 2023, with a significant bipartisan majority of 320 to 71, with one member voting present. [1, 8, 11] The legislation is designed to increase price transparency in the healthcare system by establishing new requirements for hospitals, insurers, and Pharmacy Benefit Managers (PBMs) to disclose cost, pricing, and rebate information to employers and patients. [1, 5] The bill also extends funding for several public health programs, including community health centers. [4, 5] Following its passage in the House, the bill moved to the Senate for consideration. [3] The figure represents a significant increase of 14.1 million people (a 46% increase) since 2021. [1, 7] The results, released on March 15, 2024, revealed that 94% of the nearly 1,000 responding hospitals experienced financial repercussions. [2, 5] The impact on revenue was severe, with nearly 60% of affected hospitals reporting daily losses of $1 million or more. [3, 5] Furthermore, 74% of hospitals stated that the cyberattack directly affected patient care, with some reporting delays in securing necessary care authorizations. [4, 6] More than half of the surveyed hospitals described the financial hit as 'significant or serious.' [6] This represents a slight decrease from the 36% compliance rate reported in July 2023. For the individual market, six insurance carriers have requested average rate hikes ranging from 5.0% to 11.6%, resulting in a weighted average increase of 9.3%. In the small group market, eight companies have requested increases between 5.7% and 16.3%, for a weighted average increase of 12.3%. During the hearings, each insurer will present on its requested rate changes. <2> A report by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) Office of the Actuary, published in Health Affairs, revealed that U.S. national health expenditures (NHE) grew 7.5% to $4.9 trillion in 2023. [12, 16] This marks a significant acceleration from the 4.1% growth rate observed in 2022. [1, 2, 3] The increase in 2023 was largely driven by a rise in the use and intensity of healthcare services. [12, 14] Concurrently, the insured portion of the population reached a high of 92.5% in 2023. [10] Spending on hospital care saw a notable 10.4% increase to $1.5 trillion, while physician and clinical services spending rose by 7.4% to $978.0 billion. [16] Retail prescription drug expenditures also accelerated, growing by 11.4% to $449.7 billion, influenced by treatments for diabetes and obesity. [12, 16] As a result, the share of the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) dedicated to healthcare rose to 17.6% in 2023 from 17.3% in 2022. [9, 14, 15] <3> A report from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) and the American Medical Association (AMA) confirms that U.S. health spending grew by 7.5% in 2023, reaching approximately $4.9 trillion, which equates to $14,570 per capita. This represents a significant acceleration from the 4.6% growth rate observed in 2022. metadata.original_text: This time series records healthcare costs data in the web search domain, with a collection frequency of weekly, focusing on monitoring and analyzing relevant indicators. Prediction target period: from 2025-12-21 to 2026-03-08. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On November 14, 2025, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) officially announced that the standard Medicare Part B monthly premium will increase by nearly 10% to $202.90 for the 2026 calendar year. This represents an increase of $17.90 from the 2025 premium of $185.00, marking the first time the standard base premium has exceeded $200. <2> Families USA released an analysis of 2026 health insurance rate filings, projecting an average 26% increase in individual market health insurance premiums across the United States for the upcoming plan year. <3> Willis Towers Watson (WTW) has released its 2026 Global Medical Trends report, forecasting that US healthcare costs will rise by 9.6% in 2026. According to the report, the significant increase in medical inflation is primarily driven by the introduction of new medical technologies, regional pressures on pharmacy and outpatient services, and structural shifts in healthcare delivery. <4> According to WTW's 2026 Global Medical Trends report, global health insurance costs are projected to increase by 10.3% in 2026, continuing a trend of steep cost hikes in recent years. In North America, medical inflation is expected to see a slight decrease from 9.4% to 9.2%, with U.S. healthcare costs specifically projected to be 9.6% in 2026. The primary driver for the global increase, cited by 74% of insurers, is the introduction of new medical technologies. Other significant factors include the decline of public health systems and advancements in pharmaceuticals. The report also identifies cancer as the fastest-growing and most expensive diagnosis influencing costs for insurers. <5> The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) released a fact sheet on October 30, 2025, projecting premium information for Health Insurance Marketplace plans on HealthCare.gov for the 2026 plan year. The projection indicates that the average premium for the lowest-cost plan, after tax credits, is expected to be $50 per month for eligible enrollees. This represents a $13 increase from the 2025 average. However, this projected premium is still $20 lower than the average monthly premium after tax credits in 2020, before the COVID-19 pandemic. The open enrollment period for the 2026 plan year is scheduled to run from November 1, 2025, to January 15, 2026. <6> A KFF analysis projects that if the enhanced premium tax credits, which were extended through 2025 by the Inflation Reduction Act, are not renewed, average annual premium payments for subsidized enrollees in the Affordable Care Act (ACA) marketplace could more than double in 2026. Specifically, the analysis estimates a 114% increase, with average annual payments rising from $888 in 2025 to $1,904 in 2026, an average increase of $1,016 per person. These enhanced tax credits, first introduced in 2021, expanded eligibility and increased financial aid, leading to a significant rise in marketplace enrollment. The potential expiration of these subsidies at the end of 2025 has prompted debate in Congress, with the Congressional Budget Office estimating it would cost approximately $350 billion over a decade to make them permanent. <7> On September 26, 2025, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) released data on 2026 Medicare Advantage (MA) and Medicare Part D plans. The announcement indicated that average premiums are expected to remain stable or decrease. Specifically, the average monthly premium for Medicare Advantage plans is projected to decrease from $16.40 in 2025 to $14.00 in 2026. This information was released ahead of the annual Medicare open enrollment period, which runs from October 15, 2025, to December 7, 2025. <8> A report published on September 25, 2025, by the Urban Institute and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, projects significant financial strain on the U.S. healthcare system if the enhanced Affordable Care Act (ACA) premium tax credits expire at the end of 2025. The analysis forecasts that healthcare providers, including hospitals and physicians, would lose $32.1 billion in revenue in 2026. This revenue loss would be composed of reduced spending on hospital services ($14.2 billion), prescription drugs ($5.8 billion), physician services ($5.1 billion), and other healthcare services ($6.9 billion). In addition to lost revenue, providers would face a projected $7.7 billion increase in uncompensated care costs. The expiration of the tax credits is expected to cause 7.3 million people to lose their subsidized ACA coverage, resulting in 4.8 million people becoming uninsured in 2026. <9> On September 2, 2025, the U.S. Commerce Department initiated a Section 232 national security investigation into the imports of a wide range of medical supplies. The probe is intended to assess the impact of these imports on the domestic healthcare supply chain and national security, and could result in new tariffs or other import restrictions. The investigation's scope includes personal protective equipment (PPE) like surgical masks and gloves, medical consumables such as syringes and catheters, and durable medical equipment like hospital beds and pacemakers. The official notice and request for public comments was announced on September 24, 2025, and published in the Federal Register on September 26, 2025, with a comment period open until October 17, 2025. <10> The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) and the Joint Committee on Taxation (JCT) released an estimate on September 18, 2025, detailing the budgetary and coverage impacts of repealing certain health insurance marketplace provisions within the 2025 reconciliation act. The analysis projects that such a repeal would lead to a $271.9 billion increase in federal deficits over the 2026 to 2035 period. Concurrently, the number of individuals with health insurance is expected to rise, with an estimated 2.9 million more people gaining coverage by 2035 as a result of the repeal.
